newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - ABB Project Finance critical for success.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - ABB Project Finance critical for success.

text.p: ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG may be best known for its electrical engineering skills, but financial engineering is critical to its success.
With cash-strapped governments looking to the private sector to pay for infrastructure projects, companies like ABB must be able to offer competitive financing to win contracts.
"What is decisive to a high degree in winning a contract is financing," Gunnar Johannesson, president of ABB's Project and Trade Finance Group (PTF) said in an interview.
"If I can arrange a 20 year credit for the client and our competitors can do it with seven years, then ABB has a tremendous advantage," he told Reuters.
PTF, which employs 140 people worldwide and 35 at its headquarters in Zurich, is responsible for arranging financing for new power plants and other projects within ABB.

Johannesson, a dynamic Swede who proudly describes PTF as one of world leaders in industrial project finance, stressed that the group's main function is to support ABB's sales by arranging project financing, equity participations and countertrade.
PTF's importance to ABB has been growing rapidly since the mid-1980s and in 1995 PTF arranged financing for close to 40 percent of all ABB's large orders, up from 14 percent in 1990.
Judged against the world's top arrangers of financing for power projects, PTF could be rated among the top 10 investment banks.

The latest project being wrapped up by PTF is financing for the $1.6 billion Jorf Lasfar power complex, Morocco's first privately financed power plant. Once the contract is completed, it will serve as a model for ABB to secure similar deals.
PROJECT FINANCE CRITICAL TO EXPORT-DRIVEN ABB

As an export-driven company, project finance has been critical to ABB since the Latin American debt crisis in the 1980s when banks discovered sovereign default and companies learned that export credits were not without risk.
Since then risk management and project finance are two sides of the same coin.
While PTF's mandate is to support sales with attractive financing packages, it must also minimise the company's financial exposure to any defaults by its clients.

ABB's policy is that those responsible for sales must address financial exposure up front and find a solution with PTF. The exposure can then be passed on to banks, insurance companies and other institutions that are specialists in risk handling.

"One of the reasons we are so successful is that the sales person who originates the risk for ABB is ultimately reponsible. That makes people rather concerned over how they can address this." Johannesson said.
ABB's risk reduction policy appears to bearing fruit.
In 1995 PTF closed some 90 projects worth more than $5.0 billion. But if all 90 projects were to collapse, ABB's exposure would be less than $10 million and is already provided for.
This contrasts with the 1980s when ABB's exposure to the same volume of business would have been at least $600 million.
DECLINING ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN INFRASTRUCTURE PROJECTS
The growing importance of project finance not only reflects the diminishing role governments play in societies' infrastructure, but also a new economic environment.
Up to the 1990s, state agencies would set specifications for a project and ask companies to bid for individual parts, such as turbines or locomotives. It was a piecemeal approach.
Now, customers look for total solutions, such as a regional power system, from generation to distribution. Such solutions are much more expensive, thus increasing the role of financing.
As an example, ABB now sells to a private Independent Power Producer (IPP) who has secured an agreement with a distributor to deliver electricity at a certain price.
The brand of turbine will not make a major difference in meeting this price. The critical elements are financing terms, such as length of the credit, interest and security.
"Technically, our competition is acting within the same range. But who can finance the project so the price of electricity is six cents per kilowatt instead of seven cents?" Johannesson said.
His dilemma is that countries with a huge need for infrastructure often are lacking money and credit worthiness.

Despite their love affair with emerging markets, investors run scared when confronted with serious political risks, a harsh reality Johannesson faces when trying to drum up money for a power plant or rail project in many developing countries.

PTF therefore has to identify national export credit agencies or international agencies, such as the World Bank, that are willing to underwrite the political risks and match this with a project that can entice private investors.
Much of Johannesson's time is spent convincing politicians in ABB's major production countries about the importance of competitive and strong export credit systems to support its domestic industries.
With its global presence ABB can tap into several export credit agencies and, if necessary, reallocate production to the countries offering the best export or soft credits.
CHALLENGE TO MATCH RISK TAKERS WITH CAPITAL MARKETS
Johannesson's challenge is to match the political risk takers with the capital markets that have the money.

Normally PTF collaborates with investment banks to tap the markets, but increasingly Johannesson is seeing a direct approach by capital market players, such as pension funds and insurance companies as project lenders.
A great challenge will be to increase the percentage of money under global management to be invested in projects.

Before Johannesson goes to banks or pension funds, PTF assembles a Preliminary Information Memorandum, a sophisticated piece of financial engineering that provides full details of the project's financial structure, including risks.

The development of a memorandum unloads a lot of hard work for the investment banks and also helps ABB to better screen the projects and direct it toward those with the highest probability of success.
"Our task is two-fold. One is to bring successful projects to closing, but also identify non-flyers early," he said.
The work put into the memorandum also increases the odds that ABB's potential projects can find investors.
Industry-wide there is only a 15 to 20 percent chance of opportunities ever materialising.
However, when PTF has screened and developed a project and presents it to the market in the form of a memorandum, Johannesson believes the hit ratio is closer to 50 percent.

"The earlier we identify the 80 percent that normally fail, the more we can optimise ABB's resources. It's important to get in early and identify why a project can't fly before too much money has been invested and it is difficult to pull out," Johannesson said.
